claims.text: The bar starts on the floor; take an overhand grip slightly wider than shoulder width and set the hips like a deadlift, a little higher.

quotes.text: With the barbell on the floor, set up with a slightly wider than shoulder-width grip. Set your hips as you would for a deadlift, but a little higher.
quotes.where: How to Do the Pendlay Row: Set Up

quotes.text: Traditional barbell rows and Pendlay rows are performed with an overhand grip
quotes.where: FAQs: Should Pendlay rows be overhand or underhand?

claims.text: The upper body stays parallel to the floor, shoulders and hips level, through the whole rep.

quotes.text: To maintain the proper positioning, keep your upper body parallel to the floor. Your shoulders and hips should be horizontally stacked at all times.
quotes.where: Trainer Tips on Form: Keep Your Chest Parallel to the Floor

claims.text: Every rep starts from the floor and ends with the bar lowered slowly and set down at a dead stop.

quotes.text: Slowly lower the barbell to the floor and place it down at a dead stop in the starting position.
quotes.where: How to Do the Pendlay Row, step 5

quotes.text: you put the bar back on the floor between each repetition
quotes.where: Commentary

claims.text: Only the bar and arms move: the upper body stays still while the bar is pulled as high as it will go, to the abs or chest.

quotes.text: Pull the bar towards you, without otherwise moving your upper body. Pull the bar as high as you can, so that it touches your abs or chest if possible.
quotes.where: How to Do Pendlay Rows, step 2

quotes.text: Only the bar and your arms are moving
quotes.where: Commentary

claims.text: Brace, then pull the bar explosively to the base of the chest without shrugging the shoulders or letting the hips come forward.

quotes.text: Brace your core and use your lats to explosively pull the barbell to the base of your chest. Make sure not to elevate your shoulders or allow your hips to come forward.
quotes.where: How to Do the Pendlay Row: Brace and Pull

claims.text: A named fault is raising the back angle (standing partly up) to yank the bar; it probably means the load is too heavy.

quotes.text: Just as you might be tempted to partially stand straight up during the Pendlay row, you might try to yank with your arms.
quotes.where: Common Pendlay Row Mistakes: Back Angle

quotes.text: If you feel like you have to dramatically raise your back angle or yank the weight up, you’ve probably slapped too many plates on the bar.
quotes.where: Common Pendlay Row Mistakes: Going Too Heavy

claims.text: Learn the form with a light weight first, then add weight gradually once the target reps are met, in steps of about 2-10% once the target is beaten by one or two reps.

quotes.text: To avoid this, lock down your Pendlay row form with light weight before advancing your load.
quotes.where: Common Pendlay Row Mistakes: Back Angle

quotes.text: When you hit your target number, then go back and gradually add more weight.
quotes.where: Common Pendlay Row Mistakes: Going Too Heavy

quotes.text: When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.
quotes.where: abstract

claims.text: Starting with a rounded back is a named risk; if you cannot reach the bar with a flat back, raise the bar on blocks or plates.

quotes.text: Initiating the Pendlay row with a rounded back diminishes the amount of power you’re able to generate, but it’s also dangerous
quotes.where: Common Pendlay Row Mistakes: Rounding Your Back

quotes.text: consider using blocks, weight plates, or a weightlifting platform to elevate the bar and reduce the distance between you and the barbell.
quotes.where: Common Pendlay Row Mistakes: Rounding Your Back

claims.text: Elbows flared wide out to the sides can put the shoulders in a compromising position; lighten the load until it stops, and cue the elbows into the pockets or the bar to the hips.

quotes.text: But completely “chicken-winging” your elbows out to the sides can put your shoulders in a compromising position.
quotes.where: Common Pendlay Row Mistakes: Flaring Your Elbows

quotes.text: If you feel yourself yanking the bar and splaying your elbows out to the sides, lighten the load until the problem diminishes.
quotes.where: Common Pendlay Row Mistakes: Flaring Your Elbows

quotes.text: You can also try cueing yourself to put your elbows in your pockets or to pull the bar to your hips.
quotes.where: Common mistakes: Flaring Your Elbows

claims.text: Both feet stay flat and firmly planted, about shoulder width, with the knees slightly bent to reach the bar; heels lifting mid-lift: use a lighter weight.

quotes.text: Stand over a loaded barbell with your feet shoulder-width apart.
quotes.where: How to Do the Pendlay Row, step 1

quotes.text: Start with your body hinged forward, back flat, core tight, and knees slightly bent so you can grip the bar.

claims.text: The main movers are the lats, traps and rear delts, with the biceps, lower back, forearm flexors and rotator cuff as secondary muscles; the hamstrings and spinal erectors hold the bent-over position.

plate.viewWhy: The level torso, the bar path from floor to chest, the rounded back at the start (the top fault, c8, c23) and the back-angle rise all happen front-to-back (c2, c4, c6); the census draws it side, like the parent.
plate.equipment: Straight barbell with plates resting on the floor line at the start (c1, c3).
plate.start: Hips hinged a little higher than a deadlift (c1), torso parallel to the floor with shoulders and hips level (c2), knees slightly bent, feet about shoulder width (c10), arms straight down to the bar on the floor (c3).
plate.end: Same torso and hip angle (c4); bar touching the base of the chest or abs (c4, c5).

mistake.what: Back rounded at the start: the lifter reaches the bar with a rounded back.
mistake.why: Starting the row with a rounded back is dangerous (c8): too much spinal flexion leaves the back open to shear forces that may lead to pain, strains or disc herniations (c23).
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 2: the rounded back at the start (c8, c23). Step 1: no frequency word counts for a fault. Set aside: GGR's "Here are the most common mistakes associated with the Pendlay row" and BarBend's "you’re bound to run into some common mistakes" are a list heading and a list sentence; GGR's "the barbell may pull you forward off your heels, typically during the eccentric phase of the movement" says when, not how often; "increasing weight too quickly often works against you" is about the load; BarBend's "the Pendlay row is more advanced for most beginners" is about the exercise; the NHS lines ("Back pain, particularly lower back pain, is very common.", "A common cause of back pain is an injury like a pulled muscle (strain).") are about back pain in general, with no fault. Step 2: two faults on GGR's common-mistakes list are tied to harm. The rounded back: "it’s also dangerous" (c8) and "Too much spinal flexion or extension leaves the back susceptible to shear forces that may lead to pain, strains, or disc herniations" (c23). Flared elbows: "it puts the shoulders in a potentially dangerous position, which may lead to pain or a shoulder injury" (GGR). Both are on a common-mistakes list; one source ties each to harm (BarBend's "can put your shoulders in a compromising position", c9, names no injury, pain, stress or discomfort, so it is not counted); both are sourced directly; GGR's list names the rounded back first, so it wins. GGR's heels line ("it also is important for preventing injuries") is about controlling the lowering and comes third on the same list. Standing partly up to yank (c6), the head's pick until now, states no harm (BarBend's Back Angle and Going Too Heavy sections). Set aside as not about a fault: BarBend's "minimizing injury risk" (back exercises in general) and "completely removes any stress on your lower back" (the seal row); Fenwick's "produced the largest lumbar spine load" (c18, the exercise). drawable stays true: the rounded back is a still sign the side view shows. Pick changed: standing partly up to yank is now handlingMistakes[1].

tells.text: Bar rests on the floor each rep
Back stays level as the bar rises

tempo.text: Up 1 and down 2 keep ACSM's 1-2 s, stated for intermediate to advanced training (c14, WEAK; LR-15). The dead stop on the floor between reps (c3, c14) is at the bottom, not right after the pull, so pause is 0 (LR-33); no source gives its seconds. GGR's "Squeeze the contraction at the top of the movement." asks for no pause length and no brief or momentary hold, so it sets no pause.

grip.handContact: Bar across the base of the fingers and top of the palm (pull archetype); straps allowed when the grip gives out first.
grip.wrist: Bent back into its natural grip position (about 35 degrees), not curled forward; grip weakens when the wrist moves away from it.

Bar on the floor. Stand over it, feet shoulder width.
Hips a little above deadlift height. Overhand grip, slightly wider than shoulders.
Back rounds to reach it? Raise the bar on blocks or plates.
Beat target by one or two reps? Add 2 to 10 percent.

libraryDiff.why: Library primary mid_back and secondary lats, biceps, rear_delts, with lower_back as stabiliser, fit the sources (c11 names lats, traps and rear delts as primary; the card shows lats as a primary feel, as the parent does). Hamstrings hold the position isometrically (c11); shown as a watch feel only, not proposed for the library list.

notes: Drawing conventions (LR-4; LR-34 way 2; R-LB3-5): grip.handContact ("Bar across the base of the fingers and top of the palm (pull archetype); straps allowed when the grip gives out first.") and the drawn palm direction (palms down, as grip.type states from c1) are drawing conventions, not claims. The drawn wrist, grip.wrist ("Bent back into its natural grip position (about 35 degrees), not curled forward; grip weakens when the wrist moves away from it."), is this card's convention until the hand lane decides the hold and pull wrists across cards (F-LB3-3).
